senses: towards (a person or, more rarely, a thing)
to, towards, with respect to, with regard to, concerning, about
la:prep:erga.html:
ergā,
praep. [syncop. for e-regā, from ex and root rag-, to reach upward, be upright; cf. ergo, v. Corss. Ausspr. 1, 448 sqq.], over against, opposite to (cf.: adversus, versus, contra, e regione, e contrario).
Lit., of locality (ante- and post-classical and rare): quae med erga aedes habet,i. e. opposite me, (al. modo erga): erga regiam,.—
Trop.: aliquem, more rarely aliquid, of feelings and conduct towards a person.
Of friendly feelings, etc. (so mostly in class. lang.): erga et in hoc differunt: fere enim erga ad affectum refertur, quasi erga illum benignus: in ad simultatem, quasi in illum sum saevus, P.; cf. : ut eodem modo erga amicum affecti simus,

quo erga nosmet ipsos ... ut nostra in amicos benevolentia illorum erga nos benevolentiae pariter respondeat, ; cf. ; ; : erga aliquem benevolus,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. : divina bonitas erga homines,: perpetua erga populum Romanum fides,; cf. ; et saep.: te oro per mei te erga bonitatem patris,; so, te erga,: med erga,: se erga,: amicum erga,; cf. the following.—Relating to things: cum in universam rem publicam, tum etiam erga meam salutem fide ac benevolentia singulari,; cf. ; ; —

Of unfriendly feelings, for the usual contra or adversus, against: ne malus item erga me sit, ut illum erga fuit,; ; ; ; : odium, quod erga regem susceperant,; ; ; ; ; ; cf. transp.: med erga,; ; .—Relating to things: res secundae valent commutare naturam, et raro quisquam erga bona sua satis cautus est,against his own advantage,.—
In post-Aug. authors (esp. in Tacitus) in gen. of every kind of mental relation to a person or thing, to, towards, in respect to: anxii erga Sejanum, cujus durior congressus,: erga Germanicos exercitus laudes gratesque,; : prisco erga duces honore,fin.; cf. : suprema erga memoriam filii sui munera,; : atrociore semper fama erga dominantium exitus,; ; v. Hand Turs. II. pp. 437-440.

la:verb:ergo.html:
ergō (rarely with short
o in Ov. and the post-Aug. poets, Lennep.; ; ; ; ), adv.
for e-regō, from ex and root rag-, to extend upward; cf. Gr. ὀρέγω, L. rego, Germ. ragen; v. erga, and Corss. Ausspr. 1, 448 sqq.
, proceeding from or out of.
With gen. (placed after it, like causa and gratia), in consequence of, on account of, because of (ante-class, but not in Plaut. or Ter.): quojus rei ergo,: hujus rei ergo, § 3; 4; ; Tab. Publica ap. ; fin.: dono militari virtutis ergo donari, S. C. ap. ; so, virtutis ergo, Lex ap. ; Sisenn. ap. : ejus victoriae ergo, Inscr. ap. : funeris ergo, Lex ap. ; fin.: ejus legis ergo,; Quadrig. ap. : formidinis ergo,: illius ergo,.
Absol. (for cujus rei ergo), consequently, accordingly, therefore, then (class.): unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem: ergo postque magisque viri nunc gloria claret, Enn. ap. ; Lucil. ap. ; : Polemoni et jam ante Aristoteli ea prima visa sunt, quae paulo ante dixi. Ergo nata est sententia veterum Academicorum, etc.,: Albano non plus animi erat quam fidei, nec manere ergo, nec transire aperte ausus, etc.,; et saep.—The reason or cause sometimes follows with quia, quod: ergo istoc magis, quia vaniloquus, vapulabis,; cf. .—Ante- and postclass. pleonast.: ergo igitur,; and: igitur ergo, —So in Ter. and Liv.: itaque ergo,; Drak.; 3, 31, 5 Gron.; 9, 31 fin.; 39, 25.—
Transf.
In a logical conclusion, consequently, therefore: negat haec filiam me suam esse: non ergo haec mater mea est,; ; ; ; 59 sq. al.: nullum dicere causae esse genus amentia est, etc. ... Relinquitur ergo, ut omnia tria genera sint causarum,: quis est enim, in quo sit cupiditas, quin recte cupidus dici possit? Ergo et avarus erit, sed finite,; : quis tam esset ferreus qui eam vitam ferre posset, etc.? Verum ergo illud est, quod a Tarentino Archyta dici solitum, et saep.; corresponding to igitur,fin. and 15 init.; so consecutively, igitur ... ergo ... ergo ... igitur ... —So with si, cum, quia, etc.: ergo ego nisi peperissem, Roma non oppugnaretur,; ; ; . —So esp. in Cicero, like an (v. an I. D.), in interrogative argumentation, a minore ad majus, or ex aequo, so, so then: ergo haec veteranus miles facere poterit, doctus vir sapiensque non poterit?; so with the future, § 41; 1, 14, 31; 3, 15, 31; ; : ergo illi intelligunt, quid Epicurus dicat, ego non intelligo?; cf. : ergo Ennio licuit vetera contemnenti dicere, etc. ... mihi de antiquis eodem modo non licebit?; cf. —
In interrogations.
When an explanation is asked, do you say? do you mean? then: S. Quo agis? P. Quo tu? ... S. Quo ergo, scelus? : Ipsus es? Ch. Ipsus Charmides sum. S. Ergo ipsusne es? ; ; .—
When a consequence is inquired for, Engl. then: Ps. lstuc ego jam satis scio. Si. Cur ergo, quod scis, me rogas? : ergo in iis adolescentibus bonam spem esse dicemus, quos? etc.,: dedemus ergo Hannibalem? dicet aliquis, et saep.: num ergo is excaecat nos aut orbat sensibus, si? etc.,; so, num ergo,; cf. : quid stamus? quin ergo imus?why not then?; so, quin ergo,; ; ; .— Esp. freq., quid ergo? like the Gr. τί οὖϝ, why then? but why? quid ergo hanc dubitas colloqui? ; cf. ; ; : quid ergo? hujusne vitae propositio Thyesten levare poterit?; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; et saep.—
With imperatives and words used imperatively, then, now, accordingly: dato ergo istum symbolum illi,: vide ergo, hanc conclusionem probaturusne sis,: desinite ergo,: sequere ergo,; ; ; cf.: amplectere ergo,: tace ergo,; : dic ergo,: ausculta ergo, ; et saep.: quin tu ergo i modo,come now, begone!; cf.: quin tu ergo omitte genua,: agedum ergo,.—So with the subj.: age eamus ergo, intro ergo abeant,; : abeamus ergo intro,: ergo des minam,; ; .—And with the future: ergo, si sapis, mussitabis,.—
Like igitur, in resuming an interrupted train of thought, as I was saying; I say, then; well then: tres viae sunt ad Mutinam, quo festinat animus, ut, etc. ... Tres ergo ut dixi viae,; cf. ; ; ; .—So (like igitur and inquam) after parenthetical sentences, ; ; .—Less freq. for inquam in a mere repetition: mihi tuus pater, Pater hujus ergo, hospes Antidamas fuit,; or in beginning a subject with reference to the expectation of the auditors (cf. Gr. ἄρα), then, now: accipite ergo animis,; . See Hand Turs. II. pp. 440-467.

senses: to cause to halt, stop, because of the erect posture assumed
to arouse someone, encourage, stir up
la:verb:erigo.html:
ē-rĭgo, rexi, rectum, 3, v. a.
rego
,
to raise or set up, to erect (very freq. and class.).
Lit.
In gen.: rubrum jubar,: caput,: ar borem (with extollere),: hominem,to form erect,: os,; jacentem,: hastas,; : digitum,: manus ad tectum,; cf.: scalas ad moenia,: agmen in adversum clivum,to lead up,: cf. ; ; ; : aciem in collem,: oculos,i. e. to raise..—
With se,

or (more freq., esp. since the Aug. per.) mid., to set one's self up, to rise: connituntur (pueri), ut sese erigant,; so, sese aut sublevare (Alces),: statura breves in digitos eriguntur,i. e. raise themselves on tiptoe,; cf.: in ungues,: in armos (equus),: in auras,; : sub auras,: ad sidera (fumus), et saep.— Said of rising ground, ; ; cf. under P. a.—

In partic.
To build, construct, erect (rarely): turres,: saxeas turres,: quis totidem erexit villas,. —
Milit. t. t., to cause to halt, stop, because of the erect posture assumed: Albanus erigit totam aciem,.—
Trop.
In gen., to arouse, excite: erigite mentes auresque vestras et me attendite,; cf. aures (with animum attendere),: animos ad audiendum,: cum res relata exspectatione certaminis senatum erexisset,had aroused, excited,; cf. under P.a. B. 2.: aculeos severitatis in rem, etc.,: libertas malis oppressa civilibus extollere jam caput et aliquando se erigere debebat,: paululum se erexit et addidit historiae majorem sonum vocis,—
In partic., to raise up, cheer up, encourage: erigebat animum jam demissum et oppressum Oppianicus,; cf. ; : spem,: illam tu provinciam afflictam et perditam erexisti atque recreasti,; cf.: rempublicam, Pompeius ap. , C fin.: rempublicam ex tam gravi casu,: multos populos ad cupidinem novae fortunae,: Germanos ad spem belli, Caesarem ad coercendum,; cf. ; : Lusitanos,: fiduciam Pori,: animos ad spem, et saep.: non dubito quin tuis litteris se magis etiam erexerit ab omnique sollicitudine abstraxerit,; so, se,; ; ; ; cf.: se in spem,: se ad spem libertatis,: se ad imitationem,.—Mid., ; ; ; .—Hence, ērectus, a, um, P. a., set up; upright; elevated, lofty.
Prop.: primum eos (homines) humo excitatos celsos et erectos constituit,; cf.: erectus et celsus status,: incessus,: vultus,; and in the comp.: coxae,: viriditas culmo geniculato,: prorae,; cf.: petra in metae modum,; and in the comp., .—Sup., Jul. Valer. Res Gest. Alex. M. 1, 31.—
Trop.
Elevated, lofty, noble: celsus et erectus et ea quae homini accidere possunt omnia parva ducens,; cf. animus (with magnus),; in the comp.: erectior homo,: habet mens nostra natura sublime quiddam et erectum et impatiens superioris,; cf. .—
In a bad sense, haughty, lofty, ; cf. .—
Intent, attentive, on the stretch: judices,; cf.: suspensique (Horatii),: plebs, civitas exspectatione,; : vos ad libertatem recuperandam (with ardentes),: mens circa studia,: studium in legendo,: multitudo,; cf.: erecta in Othonem studia,lively sympathies,.—Comp.: ad agendum erectiores,.—
Animated, encouraged, resolute: legiones nostrae in eum saepe locum profectae alacri animo et erecto, unde, etc.,: nunc vero multo sum erectior,: erectis animis,.—Adv.: ērectē (acc. to B. 3.), boldly, courageously (late Lat.); in the comp.: judicare,: loqui,.

senses: to instruct, to educate; to cultivate, to refine
la:verb:erudio.html:
ē-rŭdĭo, īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a., qs. to free from roughness, i. e.
to polish, educate, instruct, teach (freq. and class.; cf.: doceo, edoceo, praecipio, instituo).
Prop.: studiosos discendi erudiunt atque docent,: aliquem, (with docere); (with instituere); ; Quint. prooem. § 1; 6 et saep.: filios ad majorum instituta (with instituere),; cf. : aliquem artibus,; cf. : eum ad exquisitissimam consuetudinem Graecorum erudiit,: aliquem in jure civili,; cf. .—With two acc. (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): aliquem leges praeceptaque belli,; cf. ; v. also under P. a.: aliquem, with an object-clause, ; cf. without aliquem,; .—With a rel.-clause as object: qua possint arte capi,: tirones neque in ludo, neque per lanistas,i. e. to cause to be instructed,: gladiatores sub eodem magistro eruditi,: Athenas erudiendi gratia missus,; once: aliquem de aliqua re, Cic.: obviae mihi velim sint tuae litterae, quae me erudiant de omni re publica,instruct me, keep me informed of,.—
Transf., of objects not personal: artes,: ut flerent, oculos erudiere suos,; : Polycletus consummasse hanc scientiam judicatur et toreuticen sic erudisse, ut Phidias aperuisse,to have cultivated, brought to perfection,.— Hence, ērŭdītus, a, um, P. a., learned, accomplished, well-informed, skilled, experienced (cf.: litteratus, doctus, peritus, gnarus, scitus).
Prop.: est non satis politus iis artibus, quas qui tenent eruditi appellantur,: Graeculus otiosus et loquax, et fortasse doctus atque eruditus,: semper mihi et doctrina et eruditi homines placuerunt,; : nec sicut vulgus sed ut eruditi solent appellare sapientem,; cf. opp. rusticus,; et saep.: non transmarinis nec importatis artibus eruditi, sed genuinis domesticisque virtutibus,: homines non litteris ad rei militaris scientiam, sed rebus gestis ac victoriis eruditos,; ; cf. ; ; : eruditi Socraticis disputationibus,: a pueris eruditi artibus militiae, et saep.; cf. in the comp.: litteris eruditior quam Curio,; and in the sup.: Scaevola, homo omnium et disciplina juris civilis eruditissimus,.— With acc.: Graecas res eruditi,; cf. .—With inf.: eruditus utilia honestis miscere,.—
Transf., of inanimate and abstract subjects: quod ceteri minus eruditis hominum seculis fuerunt,: tempora (with docti homines),: aures,; ; : animus,: oratio (opp. popularis), id. Par. prooem. § 4; cf. ; : Graecorum copia,fulness of Greek learning,: palata, i. e. practised, fine (with docta), ; cf. gustus,.—In neutr. with a subject-clause: ex historia ducere urbanitatem, eruditum est,; cf.: eruditissimum longe, si, etc.,.— Adv.: ērŭdītē, learnedly, eruditely.— Comp., ; .— Sup., ; .
la:verb:erudio.inflection: īvi or ii, ītum, 4, v. a.

la:noun:erus.gloss: master of the house or family
senses: master of the house or family
a spouse, husband; an owner; a ruler, sovereign; a divinity, god
la:noun:erus.html:
ĕrus (less correctly, hĕrus,
v.infra), i, m.
Sanscr. root, har-; har-āmi, I seize; har-anam, hand; Gr. χείρ, χέρης; Lat. heres, hirudo; but the form erus is that of the best MSS.; cf. Ritschl, Opusc. 2, 409; Brix ad
.
Lit., the master of a house or family, in respect to servants: erum atque servom saluere,: iis, qui vi oppressos imperio coercent, sit sane adhibenda saevitia, ut eris in famulos, si aliter teneri non possunt, ; cf.: non eros nec dominos appellabant eos, quibus juste paruerunt,; : me meus erus Fecit ut vigilarem,: nonne erae meae nunciare, quod erus meus jussit, licet?: quis erus est igitur tibi?; 225: nec victoris eri tetigit captiva cubile,; ; cf.: O ere, quae res Nec modum habet, etc.,: Le. Ubinam est erus? Li. Major apud forum'st minor hic est intus, our old ... our young master, ; cf. —
Transf.
Of men, a master, lord, owner, proprietor (poet.): agellulum hunc erique villulam hortulumque pauperis Tuor,; cf.: propriae telluris erus,; and: ne perconteris, fundus meus Arvo pascat erum, an, etc.,: destinata Aula divitem manet erum,: O cubile ... quae tuo veniunt ero Quanta gaudia,.—
Of the gods: nondum cum sanguine sacro Hostia caelestes pacificasset eros,.—Of the gods, absol.: quod temere invitis suscipiatur eris,.

senses: alternative form of aerō (“wicker basket; hamper”)

ĕra (less correctly, hera; v. erus), ae (archaic

erus

(Trag. v. 287 Vahl.): servus Dat (puellam) erae suae,; so ; 2, 8, 70; ; ; ; . So, era major and era minor, the old and young mistress, the lady of the house and her daughter, and 23.—
Meton., a mistress, female ruler or governor.
Of goddesses: domina, era (Minerva), Enn. ap. Ach. (Vahl. , no. 22): Fortuna, era, dub.; cf.: vosne velit an me regnare era quidve ferat Fors, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 203 Vahl.—for which, sit sane Fors domina campi, ): rapidi Tritonis era,i. e. Minerva,: hilarate erae (i. e. Cybeles) citatis erroribus animum,; so : tergeminam tunc placat eram (Hecaten),: noctis eram Ditemque ciens,i. e. Proserpine,.—
Of sweethearts, ; so .

senses: delusion (a departing from the truth), misunderstanding
la:noun:error.html:
error, ōris, m.
id.
,
a wandering.
In gen., a wandering, straying or strolling about (rare and mostly poet.).
Lit.: ad quos Ceres in illo errore venisse dicitur,: error ac dissipatio civium (sc. mercatorum), Mos. (cf. erratio, I.): navium pars ex errore eodem conferebatur, Auct. B. Afr. 11; cf. ; ; ; ; et saep.—Transf., of the motion of atoms, ; of the meanderings of rivers, ; of the mazes of the labyrinth, ; 167.—
Trop., a wavering, uncertainty: fluctuat incertis erroribus ardor amantum,:

nec, quid corde nunc consili capere possim, Scio, tantus cum cura meo est error animo, ; cf. ; ; ; ; so, too, with obj. gen.: viarum,uncertainty, ignorance,; cf. veri,.—

In partic., a wandering from the right way, a going astray.
Lit. (very seldom): reduxit me usque ex errore in viam,; —
Trop., a departing from the truth, an error, mistake, delusion (class.; cf.: erratum, vitium, peccatum): erroris ego illos et. dementiae complebo,: opinionibus vulgi rapimur in errorem nec vera cernimus,; cf.: inducere imperitos in errorem,; : errore quodam fallimur in disputando,: si errorem velis tollere,: errorem tollere,; : deponere,: eripere alicui,: demere, et saep.: mentis,i. e. distraction, insanity,; cf. ; ; so poet. of other kinds of mental perturbation, as fear, ; love,; ; cf. ; : aut aliquis latet error; equo ne credite, Teucri,some deception,; cf. : par forma aut aetas errorem agnoscentibus fecerat,: jaculum detulit error in Idam,.—
Esp., an error in language, a solecism, .—
Rarely a moral error, fault (cf. erro, I. B. 2.), ; cf. ; 2, 3, 92.—
Error, personif., = Ἄτη, the inspirer of folly or judicial blindness, .

senses: to snatch, snatch away, take away, tear out, pull out, pluck, rob
to die suddenly, to be suddenly taken away, to be suddenly snatched away
la:verb:eripio.html:
ē-rĭpĭo, ĭpŭi, eptum, 3, v. a.
rapio
,
to snatch, tear, or pull out; to snatch away, take away (freq. and class.; cf.: capio, prehendo, sumo, demo, adimo, rapio, furor).
Lit.
In gen.: tibias ex ore,; cf.: bolum e faucibus,: hirundines ex nido,; : ex manibus alicujus, Cass. ap. ; : torrem ab igne,: ensem vaginā, et saep.: aliena bona, ; so, vela, armamenta, copias,; ; : nubem,: purgamenta hortorum,to carry away, et saep.: aliquem, etc.,to deliver, set free,; ; ; ; cf.: aliquem e manibus hostium,; ; : Abydenos ex obsidione,: aliquem ex periculo,; cf.: istum fortuna ex illo periculo eripuit,: aliquem ex vinculis,: aliquem ex miseriis, Crassus ap. : aliquem ex media morte,; cf.: filium a morte,: praedam de manibus,: istum de vestra severitate,; but: ex severitate alicujus,, § 83: aliquem malis,: erepto ex equo C. Flaminio,: oculum alicui,; : gladium isti,: classem Caesari,: concubinam militi,: aliquem (aliquam) alicui,; ; ; ; —Less freq.: aliquem ab aliquo,; ; ; so, ereptis ab eo duabus legionibus,: a Trisensibus plus lucri,; . —
With se, to take one's self off, to flee, escape: per eos, ne causam diceret, se eripuit,: se latebris,fin.; cf.: se ex manibus militum,fin.: se ab illa miseria,: se ex pugna,; ; : se sequentibus,: se hosti fugā,: se flammā,: se leto,: se flammis,: se morae,: se servituti,: rebus humanis se, et saep.—With adv.: eas inde,.—
Prov.: Lupo agnum eripere, for something difficult or impossible,.—
Pregn.: eripi, to be snatched away by death, to die suddenly (not before the Aug. per.): fatis erepta,: primis conjux ereptus in annis,; cf.: in flore aetatis ereptus rebus humanis,.—Rarely act.: lux ereptura eum vitā,; cf. 30, 5, 10.
Trop., to take away, snatch away: responsiones omnes hoc verbo,; cf.: orationem alicui ex ore,: primam vocem ab ore loquentis,: alicui jus suum,: libertatem (hostis),; cf. : potestatem hominis omnino aspiciendi (opp. suppeditare omnium rerum abundantiam),; cf. : omnem usum navium,: semestre imperium,; cf.: tetrarchiam alicui,: mihi dolorem,: alicui errorem,; cf. ; ; : alicui timorem,; : lucem,; fin.; et saep.: alicui pudicitiam,; but: virginis pudorem,; cf.: caelumque diemque Teucrorum ex oculis,; and: prospectum oculis,: tempora certa modosque,: jocos, venerem, etc. (anni),: vatibus omnem fidem,: fugam, poet. for se fuga, or for the simple rapere fugam, to flee, .—Poet.: eripiunt flammae noctem, i. c. light up the night, : eripuere oculos aurae,: se fluvius retro eripit,turns back,.—Poet., with an object clause: posse loqui eripitur,: illis eriperes verbis mihi, sidera caeli Lucere,i. e. to persuade me that not,.—With quin: vix tamen eripiam, velis quin, etc., I shall scarcely hinder you from, etc., .

senses: to err, wander from the truth, to mistake
la:verb:erro.html:
erro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
[root er-, to go; desiderative forms, ἔρχομαι (ἐρσκ-); and Lat. (ers-o) erro, to seek to reach; hence, to wander; cf. Germ. irren; Engl. err, etc., v. ].
Neutr.
In gen.
Prop., to wander, to wander or stray about, to wander up and down, to rove (freq. and class.; cf. vagor, palor): propter te errans patria careo,; cf.: cum vagus et exsul erraret,: ignari hominumque locorumque Erramus vento huc et vastis fluctibus acti,; cf. ; 3, 200; ; et saep.: circum villulas nostras,: pios per lucos,: inter audaces lupus errat agnos,; cf. of beasts,; ; ; ; ; et saep.—Pass. impers.: male tum Libyae solis erratur in agris,.—Prov.: in media luce errare,.—
Transf., of inanimate things: (stellae) quae errantes et quasi vagae nominantur,; so of the planets,; ; ; ; ; cf. of the motion of the stars in gen.,: Cocytus errans flumine languido,; cf. : errantesque per altum Cyaneae,: hic lintres errare videres,: vidi ad frontem sparsos errare capillos,i. e. flying about,; cf. : errantia lumina,i. e. moving fitfully about, (4, 13, 27 M.); cf. : pulmonibus errat Ignis edax,i. e. spreads, runs about, et saep.—
Trop., to wander, stray at random: ne vagari et errare cogatur oratio, , 48, 209; cf.: erraus et vaga sententia (opp. stabilis certaque), : eo fit, ut errem et vager latius,: ut ingredi libere, non ut licenter videatur errare,: errans opinio (opp. stabilis conscientia),: dubiis affectibus errat,: ne tuus erret honos,be in doubt, uncertain,; cf. .— Poet., with a rel.-clause: erro, quam insistas viam,I am uncertain, in doubt,; cf.: inter recens et vetus sacramentum,i. e. to hesitate, vacillate,.—
In partic., to miss the right way, to lose one's self, go astray (in the literal sense rarely, but in the trop. freq. and class.).
Lit.: homo qui erranti comiter monstrat viam, Enn. ap. : errare viā,: maledictus qui errare facit caecum in itinere,.—
Trop., to wander from the truth, to err, mistake: avius errat Saepe animus,; cf. : totā erras viā,; cf.: in eo non tu quidem totà re, sed temporibus errasti,: longe,; cf. procul, Kritz. N. cr.: errant probe,: vehementer,: valde, et saep.: errare malo cum Platone quam cum istis vera sentire,; cf. : erras, si id credis,; so with si, ; ; et saep.: de nostris verbis errat,: in aliqua re,; ; : in alteram partem,; cf.: in alienos fetus,.—Less freq. with acc. of a neutr. pronoun: mone, quaeso, si quid erro,; so with quid, ; ; ; : hoc,.—Poet. also with the acc. of a noun: errabant tempora,i. e. in chronology,.— Pass. impers.: si fuit errandum,: si nihil esset erratum,: si erratur in nomine,; cf.: tutius circa priores erratur,: uno verbo esse erratum,. —Sometimes, in a palliative manner, of moral error, to err through mistake: pariter te errantem et illum sceleratissimum persequi,; cf. . —Hence,
errātum, i, n., an error, mistake, fault: illud de Flavio et fastis, si secus est, commune erratum est,; cf. fin.: cujus errato nulla venia, recte facto exigua laus proponitur,; : nullum ob totius vitae non dicam vitium, sed erratum,; cf. ; ; and in plur., ; ; .—
Act. in Aug. poets (only in part. perf.), to wander over or through: immensum est erratas dicere terras,: ager,: orbis,: litora,.
la:verb:erro.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

senses: to dig, tear or pluck out
la:verb:eruo.html:
ē-rŭo, ŭi, ŭtum, 3, v. a.,
to cast forth, throw out; to dig, tear, or pluck out (freq. and class.).
Lit.
In gen.: qui sciet, ubi quidque positum sit, quaque eo veniat, is, etiam si quid obrutum erit, poterit eruere,; so, aurum terrā,; cf.: caprificos sepulcris,: gemmam vadis,; : segetem ab radicibus imis,; cf.: pinum radicibus, Heyne N. cr.; and: herbam radicitus,: mortuum,: oculum,; : dentes de sinistra parte,: aquam remis,lo stir up, plough up,; cf.: sepulcra (hyaena),.—Poet. in Greek construction: eruitur oculos,his eyes are torn out, (cf. Zumpt, Gram. § 458).—
Since the Aug. per., sometimes, in partic., to root out, to destroy from the foundation: urbem totam a sedibus,; ; cf. under II. B. 2.—
Trop.
In gen., to draw out, bring out, elicit: inde tamen aliquando (servum fugitivum) eruam, Vat. ap. ; cf. : scrutari locos, ex quibus argumenta eruamus,; cf. : si quid est, quod indagaris, inveneris, ex tenebris erueris,: ex annalium vetustate eruenda est memoria nobilitatis tuae,: memoriam,: veritatem,: causam rerum et rationem,: sacra recognosces annalibus eruta priscis,: mi sicunde potes, erues, qui decem legati Mummio fuerint, et saep.: fanum erui volo; neque hoc mihi erui potest,I cannot be talked out of it,.—
In partic.
To rescue, release: propter difficultatem pecuniariam, qua erui nusquam nisi ex privatorum bonis posset,.—
To overthrow, destroy: Trojanas ut opes et lamentabile regnum Eruerint Danai,; cf. civitatem,: Thracas (with frangere gentem),.

errātus, ūs, m.
erro
,
a wandering, roving about (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): longis erratibus actus,.

ē-rēpo, psi, 3 (

Neutr., to creep out, crawl forth.
In gen., ; ; ; .—
Esp., in an upward direction, to creep or clamber up, .—Poet. transf. of a building, to rise, .—
Trop.: pecunia quoque circa paupertatem plurimum morae habet, dum ex illa erepat,.—

la:verb:erumpo.gloss: to break out (of), to burst out (of)
senses: to break out (of), to burst out (of)
la:verb:erumpo.html:
ē-rumpo, rūpi, ruptum, 3, v. a. and n.
Act., to cause to break or burst forth; to burst, sunder (rare; mostly ante-class.).
Lit.: (brassica) tumida concoquit, eadem erumpit,: ignes,; cf. ; : Achates et Aeneas erumpere nubem ardebant,: cum sanguis eruptus est,: se erumpere, in the neuter signif., to break or burst forth, ; cf.: portis se foras erumpunt,: et caput, unde altus primum se erumpit Enipeus,.—
Trop.: gaudium,: ne in me stomachum erumpant, cum sint tibi irati,; ; cf.: iram in hostes,: sic illi invidiosa conjunctio ad bellum se erupit, Cael. ap. ; .—Far more frequent and class.,
Neutr., to break out, to burst or sally forth.
Lit.
In gen.: ex castris,; cf.: ignes ex Aetnae vertice,; and: ex stagno amnes,: tempestates,: ne quo loco erumperent Pompeiani,; cf. portis,: a porta,: sive noctu, sive interdiu erumperent,; so absol., ; ; cf.: abiit, excessit, evasit, erupit,: per hostes,to break through,; cf.: inter tela hostium,: ad Catilinam,; et saep.—
In partic., to burst forth in growing, to shoot up, sprout out: folium e latere,: lentor cortice,: hordeum,: dentes,.—
Trop., to break out, to burst forth: cum illa conjuratio ex latebris atque ex tenebris erupisset,: si illustrantur, si erumpunt omnia?are disclosed,: qui ex media (oratione) erumpit,breaks away, digresses,: risus quo pacto ita repente erumpat,; cf.: aliquando vera vox,: affectus,; cf. lacrimae,: verba vi quadam veritatis, et saep.: furor,; cf.: curae privatae in certaminibus publicis erumpebant,: seditio,; : lumen dicendi per obstantia,: ut odia occulta civium in fortunas optimi cujusque erumperent,; cf. ; ; so, vitia in amicos, id. Lael

21: iracundia in naves,: conspirationes in rempublicam, et saep.: vereor ne istaec fortitudo in nervum erumpat,i. e. may end in bringing you to the stocks, Ruhnk.; cf.: aliquid in omnium perniciem,: omnia, quae per hoc triennium agitata sunt, in hos dies, in hos menses, in hoc tempus erumpunt,: elisa (vox) in illum sonum erumpit,: in aliquem voluptatis affectum,; ; ; cf.: in omne genus crudelitatis,; : rem ad ultimum seditionis erupturam,; cf.: ad majora vitia,: quorsus (dominatio) eruptura sit horremus,; cf.: huc ejus affectus, ut, etc.,.
la:verb:erumpo.inflection: rūpi, ruptum, 3, v. a. and n.

senses: to blush on account of, to be ashamed due to
la:verb:erubesco.html:
ē-rŭbesco, bŭi, 3,
v. inch. n. and a.
Neutr., to grow red, to redden.
In gen.: vidi te totis erubuisse genis,; ; . —
In partic., to redden or blush with shame, to feel ashamed.
Absol., with praepp. or abl.: erubui mecastor misera propter clamorem tuum, etc.,; : quas (voluptates) non erubescens persequitur nominatim,; ; ; ; : in aliqua re,: aliquā re,; ; ; ; cf. viro,: de sorore multum,; et saep.—
With inf. (postAug. and freq.; in , pudet enim loqui is the true reading): noli erubescere collegam habere,; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Act., with acc.: jura fidemque Supplicis erubuit,he respected,: fratres,to blush on account of, (4, 13, 20 M.): soloecismum, (dub. al. soloecismo).—In the part. fut. pass. erubescendus, a, um, of which one should be ashamed: ignes (amoris),: id urbi Romanae fore erubescendum,; ; : sentina,: causa belli,: anni domesticis cladibus,.

la:verb:erogo.gloss: to pay, pay out, expend, disburse
senses: to pay, pay out, expend, disburse
to expend or pay out money from the public treasury (after asking the consent of the people)
to expose to death, destroy, kill
to entreat, prevail on someone by entreaties
to bring, deliver or convey water from a reservoir
la:verb:erogo.html:
ē-rŏgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
Orig., a pub. law t. t., to expend, pay out money from the public treasury, after asking the consent of the people: pecunias ex aerario,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; cf.: pecuniam in classem,: in aes alienum,: unde in eos sumptus, pecunia erogaretur,; .—
Transf. beyond the pub. law sphere, to pay, pay out, disburse, expend (cf.: pendo, expendo, perpendo, pondero, solvo, luo): Tironem Curio commendes, ut ei, si quid opus erit, in sumptum eroget,: aliquid in pretium servi,: bona sua in fraudem futurae actionis,to squander,: grandem pecuniam in Tigellinum,to bequeath,; cf.: in Tiridatem erogavit,: odores, unguenta ad funus,: nihil de bonis,; cf.: aliquid ex bonis,: aliquid pro introitu, et saep.—
Trop., in Tertullian: aliquem, to expose to death, to destroy, kill: tot innocentes,; ; .—
To entreat, prevail on by entreaties: precibus erogatus,.

la:verb:eructo.html:
ē-ructo, āre, v. a.
To belch or vomit forth, to throw up (rare but class.).
Prop.: unde tu nos turpissime eructando ejecisti,: saniem eructans, ; cf. .—
Trop.: caedem sermonibus suis,i. e. to talk of murder when drunk,.—
Ingen., to cast forth, emit, exhale: Tartarus horriferos eructans faucibus aestus,: aquam,: odorem,: noxium virus,: harenam,: flammas, vaporem, fumum,.—
Esp., to utter (eccl. Lat.): abscondita,; ; ; cf. .

The Lower World, Serv.; ; ; ; , al.—Hence,

la:other:Eryx.gloss: Erice (a city and mountain in the western part of Sicily, Italy)
senses: Erice (a city and mountain in the western part of Sicily, Italy)
la:other:Eryx.html:
Ĕryx, ȳcis, m., = Ἔρυξ,

la:adv:eruditius.gloss: 106 BCE – 43 BCE, Cicero, Cato Maior De Senectute 1.3
senses: 106 BCE – 43 BCE, Cicero, Cato Maior De Senectute 1.3

106 BCE – 43 BCE, Cicero, Cato Maior De Senectute 1.3:
Quī sī ērudītius vidēbitur disputāre quam cōnsuēvit ipse in suīs librīs, attribuitō litterīs Graecīs, quārum cōnstat eum perstudiōsum fuisse in senectūte.
If [Cato] seems to discuss these matters with more learning than he usually did in his own books, you should attribute it to Greek literature — of which, as is well known, he became a devoted student in his later years.
(In De Senectute, Cicero grants Cato a Greek erudition that belies the historical figure’s staunch anti-Hellenism — a literary license only partially justified by Cato’s own use of Greek sources to compose the Origines.)
